articles.title: Just How Different Is The Odyssey from Homer’s Epic? Here Are 5 Plot Points That People Are Calling Out
articles.content:
你是否曾带着喜爱从电影院走出，或被某本书深深打动，却发现你敬重的其他人对它完全不屑一顾？这种感觉很奇怪，而目前正是《奥德赛》电影正经历的场景。网络上因知名翻译家艾米莉·威尔逊（Emily Wilson）对克里斯托弗·诺兰这部史诗电影的严厉评论而沸沸扬扬，而威尔逊的翻译正是诺兰称此电影灵感的来源。

翻译家确实对电影给予了一些好评，但公众显然仍然争先恐后地涌入影院。这部电影是当季最火爆的影片，评论普遍好评，上映两周内全球票房已超过7亿美元。但这也引发了关于改编自深受喜爱的艺术作品的电影的有趣讨论。荷马3000年前的史诗已经启发了无数影片、电视节目和文学分析，而每一件都会以不同的方式影响人们。

你见过这部电影吗？你有什么看法？如果你已经了解这首诗，那些改动和艺术创作是否让你感到不适？接下来，我将带你了解电影与史诗诗歌之间的五个关键不同点，这些不同点正在各地的象征性茶水间引发争议。继续阅读以了解人们的观点。

在荷马的史诗中，强大而有时复仇心切的神灵是核心存在，他们审判、决定命运，并惩罚那些胆敢反抗的人。（想一想那些将希腊神描绘成穿着托加袍的法官坐在奥林匹斯山的旧好莱坞电影。）诺兰采取了不同的方法，讲述了一个明显以人为中心的故事。

我们确实有雅典娜女神，由泽妮达·科尔曼（Zendaya）扮演，奥德修斯在整部电影中都会向她寻求帮助。但基本就这些了。其他神灵，从海神波塞冬到天王宙斯，化身为海洋和风暴等自然现象，折磨奥德修斯和他的水手——这些现象不仅仅针对他们，还针对电影中的其他人——而非以实体形式出现。这是刻意为之的设计。

“对我来说，重要的是我们以当时人的视角来看待这些神灵。”诺兰对《时代》杂志说，“所以他们在自然中看到神灵的证据。他们在周围的人身上寻找并发现神灵和神灵的影响。”

特洛伊木马的故事是希腊神话中最著名的故事之一，也在电影中扮演了重要角色。在开场时，我们看到一匹巨大的木马埋在特洛伊城堡外的沙子里，希腊军队已经徒劳地尝试入侵近10年。

随着电影以非线性叙事推进，我们最终了解了全世界最著名的欺骗故事：奥德修斯的士兵躲在木马里，骗特洛伊人将他们拖入特洛伊，然后（惊喜！）他们跳出来并摧毁了这座城市。但在荷马的诗中，木马仅被提及三次。而且这不在《伊利亚特》中，即荷马从同一时期的另一部主要史诗中提及。实际上，它出现在维吉尔的《埃涅阿斯纪》，而这部作品写于几百年后。

历史学家一直争论特洛伊战争是否真的发生过，至少如这三首史诗所描述的那样。当前的学术观点认为，确实发生过某种形式的特洛伊战争（或多次），在青铜器晚期。古希腊人显然相信这个故事。那么，特洛伊木马是否忠于原诗？不是，但如果没有奥德修斯的诡计——为他回家的奋斗铺平道路——我们基本上没有一部电影。

谁知道奥德修斯还有幽默感？他在电影中相当阴郁，当然如此。他对很多士兵的死亡负责，并且已经离开家庭20年。（他同样也在精神上漂泊不定。）

但在荷马的描述中，奥德修斯是个聪明人，有一个非常著名的双关语没有进入电影的最终版本。当奥德修斯和他的士兵与独眼巨人——一个只有一只眼的巨人牧羊人——有了惊险的遭遇时，独眼巨人将他们困在他的巢穴里。

在诗中，奥德修斯告诉独眼巨人他的名字是“无人”。你应该能看出接下来会发生什么：当奥德修斯最终用一根在火上烤热的木桩刺伤独眼巨人的眼睛时，这只怪物的同伴独眼巨人跑过来，问谁正在攻击他。

“无人！”独眼巨人尖叫道。由于他们并不是最聪明的怪物群体，他们便离开了。诺兰表示，他无法让这个存在了3000年的双关语起到作用，因此它被放在了剪辑室的地板上。

在仅仅10分钟内，萨曼莎·莫顿（Samantha Morton）就带走了这部电影，我打赌她将在本奖季发表许多演讲。她扮演了女巫瑟西（Circe），当奥德修斯的士兵逃离人食族（Laestrygonians）后，登上她的岛屿家园时，瑟西将他们变成了猪。

在诗中，瑟西是一个诱惑者，她戏弄士兵和他们的领袖。孤独而孤立的她在纺织轮上歌唱和纺织，与奥德修斯的妻子佩内罗珀（Penelope）形成平行，然后她用毒药让整群人陷入麻醉。但当奥德修斯没有陷入她的毒药（他已经服用了保护性抗毒剂），她爱上了他，他们都在她那里住了一年。然后她帮助士兵继续他们的旅程。

在电影中，莫顿将角色演绎得更加世故和自保。说句实话，更加恐怖。她仅在银幕上出现几分钟，我当中几分钟的眼睛都蒙住了。在几千年的时间里，瑟西被形容为危险的致命女性和现代女性赋权的象征。在这部电影中，她显然更偏向于后者。

当奥德修斯和他的士兵遇到瑟西时，他们正在逃离的人食族？在诗中，他们是文字意思上的巨人，叫做人食族（Laestrygonians或Laestrygones），他们向奥德修斯的船掷石块，摧毁了其中11艘，然后将水手拖到岸上吃掉。只有奥德修斯的船侥幸幸免。在诺兰的改编中，人食族更像是穿着盔甲的大骑士，散发出一种军事化的能量，这种能量在《奥德赛》的第十章中并不存在，他们在这里出现。

同样，在电影中，海妖也以新的形式出现。在希腊神话中，海妖用她们美妙的歌声诱惑水手走向危险——因此有了“海妖之歌”这一说法。尽管荷马的诗并没有具体描述当奥德修斯和他的士兵穿过她们的岩石家园时，海妖以何种形式出现，但历史上她们被描绘为一种鸟-人类混合体（当然，人类部分在上面）。

在诺兰的描述中，当奥德修斯被绑在船桅上以抵抗诱惑，他的士兵用蜡堵住耳朵以阻挡声音时，海妖在岩石悬崖上几乎看不见。威尔逊讥讽地称她们为“海豹女郎”，多年来，她们被描绘得更像人鱼而非鸟。无论她们是否像传统艺术绘画那样，还是以新的形式出现，结果都是相同的：这些士兵成功通过了。

说实在的，不多。观众喜爱这部电影，艺术始终是解释和批评的对象。电影中存在并令人印象深刻的主题包括回家和古希腊的xenia概念，即诺兰电影中提到的宙斯的律法。此外，这部电影美轮美奂，完全用IMAX拍摄，并且有许多大牌明星，这是让对希腊神话知之甚少的人轻松进入这一类型的好方法。

而且人们不仅仅是轻轻涉足（记住至今的7亿美元票房）。评论普遍好评，这部电影在烂番茄上获得了94%的新鲜度评级。一些文学界的大人物对威尔逊对剧本的批评提出了质疑。

普利策奖提名作者乔伊丝·卡罗尔·欧茨（Joyce Carol Oates）站出来为诺兰的解释辩护。“人们会期望一个翻译家，一个对文本负责、为文本服务的人，对其他同样真诚行事的人会稍微更加思考和尊重。”欧茨在X上写道。

我不敢假装自己和这些学者、制片人和作家一样知识渊博，但我确实喜欢这部电影，以及它将这一类型的文学和历史介绍给全新观众的事实。说到底，难道不正是如此吗？

原文来自《读者文摘》。
articles.summary:
Have you ever walked out of a movie that you (mostly) loved, or read a book that really moved you, only to hear that someone else you respect absolutely hated it? It’s a weird feeling, and it’s kind of what’s happening with The Odyssey right now. The internet is going wild over a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s epic movie by none other than Emily Wilson, whose translation of the 3,000-year-old poem Nolan says was an inspiration.

The translator did have some good things to say about the film, and clearly the public is plowing ahead to the theater regardless. The Odyssey is the biggest hit of the summer, reviews are generally fantastic, and it’s grossed over $700 million globally in less than two weeks. But it brings up an interesting discussion about movies based on beloved works of art. Homer’s 3,000-year-old poem has inspired countless movies, TV shows and literary analyses, and every single one of them will speak to people differently.

Have you seen it? What did you think? If you were already familiar with the poem, do the changes and artistic license bother you? Ahead, I’m taking you through five differences between the epic poem and the epic movie that are being debated at proverbial water coolers everywhere. Read on to see what people are saying.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

Gods and goddesses are sidelined in the movie

In Homer’s epic, powerful and sometimes vengeful deities are front and center, casting judgment, deciding fates and punishing humans who dare to defy them. (Think of all those old Hollywood movies that portrayed Greek gods as toga-wearing judges sitting on Mount Olympus.) Nolan takes a different approach, telling a decidedly human-centered tale.

We do have Athena, played by Zendaya, whom Odysseus turns to throughout the film. But that’s basically it. Other gods, from Poseidon to Zeus, manifest themselves as the sea and the storms and other natural phenomena that plague Odysseus and his men—not to mention everyone else in the film—instead of as physical beings. And that’s by design.

“For me, what was important was that we view the gods the way that people at the time might have viewed them,” Nolan told Time. “So they’re seeing evidence of the gods in nature. They’re seeking and finding gods and the influence of gods in the people around them.”

The Trojan Horse is barely mentioned in Homer’s original tale

The story of the Trojan Horse is one of the most famous in all of Greek mythology, and it plays a huge role in the movie. Right at the outset, we see a giant wooden horse buried in the sand outside the castle walls of Troy, which the Greek army has been fruitlessly trying to invade for nearly 10 years.

As the movie continues its nonlinear narrative, we eventually get the entire story of the world’s most famous deception: Odysseus’s men hide inside the horse and trick the Trojans into dragging them into Troy, where they (surprise!) pop out and destroy the city. But the horse gets only three minor mentions in Homer’s poem. And it’s not in The Iliad, the other major Homeric poem from this time period, at all. It’s actually in Virgil’s Aeneid, which was written hundreds of years later.

Historians have long debated whether the Trojan War even happened, at least as described by these three epic poems. Current scholarship comes down on the side of yes, some kind of Trojan War (or several) did occur in the Late Bronze Age. And certainly the ancient Greeks believed in the story. So is the Trojan Horse faithful to the poem? No, but without Odysseus’s deceit, which sets the stage for his struggle to return home, we wouldn’t have much of a movie at all.

Nolan’s Cyclops didn’t get to hear Odysseus’s joke

Who knew Odysseus had a sense of humor? He’s pretty dour in the movie, which … of course he is. He’s responsible for the deaths of many of his men, and he’s been away from his home and family for 20 years. (He’s also plenty adrift metaphorically as well.)

But Homer’s Odysseus is a clever one, and there’s one very famous pun that didn’t make the final cut of the film. It happens when Odysseus and his men have a terrifying encounter with the Cyclops, a one-eyed giant shepherd who traps the group in his lair.

In the poem, Odysseus tells the Cyclops his name is Nobody. I think you can see where this is going: When Odysseus eventually gouges the Cyclops’s eye with a red-hot stake that Odysseus had been heating up over the fire, the monster’s fellow Cyclopes run over and ask him who is attacking him.

“Nobody!” the Cyclops screams. And since they’re not the smartest bunch of monsters, they leave. Nolan said he just couldn’t make the 3,000-year-old pun work, so it ended up on the cutting-room floor.

Circe has completely different motivations

In just 10 minutes, Samantha Morton runs away with this film, and I’d bet my house she’ll be giving plenty of speeches this awards season. She plays Circe, a sorceress who turns Odysseus’s men into pigs when they land on her island home after escaping from the cannibalistic Laestrygonians (more on them coming up).

In the poem, Circe is a seductress who toys with the men and their leader. Lonely and isolated, she sings and weaves at her loom in a parallel to Penelope, Odysseus’s wife, before drugging the whole lot. But when Odysseus doesn’t succumb to her potion (he had taken a protective antidote), she falls in love with him, and they all end up staying with her for a year. She then helps the men continue on their journey.

In the movie, Morton plays the role as more world-weary and self-preserving. And rather frightening, to be honest. She’s on screen for mere minutes, and I spent several of them with my eyes covered. Over the millennia, Circe has been described as both a dangerous femme fatale and a modern symbol of female empowerment. In this movie, she’s definitely more of the latter.

The movie reimagines the cannibals and sirens

Those cannibals that Odysseus and his men are running from when they meet up with Circe? In the poem, they are literal giants called the Laestrygonians (or Laestrygones), who hurl boulders at Odysseus’s ships, destroying 11 of them before dragging the sailors ashore and eating them. Only Odysseus’s ship is spared. In Nolan’s retelling, the cannibals are more like large knights with armor, giving off a militaristic energy that isn’t present in Book 10 of The Odyssey, where they appear.

The sirens, similarly, take on a new form in the movie. In Greek mythology, sirens lure sailors to their peril with their beautiful voices—hence the phrase “siren’s song.” Though Homer’s poem doesn’t actually go into what form the sirens take when Odysseus and his men sail through their rocky home, historically they are depicted as being kind of a bird-woman hybrid (the woman part is on top, of course).

In Nolan’s telling, the sirens are barely visible on the rocky bluffs as Odysseus, lashed to the mast of his ship to resist temptation, and his men, who have wax in their ears to block out the sound, navigate the rocky shoals. Wilson derisively calls them seal-ladies, and over the years, they have been portrayed as more mermaid-like than birdlike. Whether they look like traditional artistic renderings or take a new form, the end result is the same: The men make it through.

So how much does all of this matter?

Honestly? Not much. Audiences love the film, and art is always subject to interpretation and critique. The overarching themes of homecoming and the ancient Greek concept of xenia, aka hospitality, which Nolan’s film calls Zeus’s Law, are present and compelling. It’s also a gorgeous film, shot entirely on IMAX, and with so many big-name stars, it’s a great way for people who don’t know much about Greek mythology to tiptoe into the genre.

And people are doing more than tiptoeing (remember that $700 million haul so far). Reviews are overwhelmingly favorable, with the film snagging a 94% fresh critics rating on Rotten Tomatoes. And some big names in the literary world are taking issue with Wilson’s panning of the script.

Joyce Carol Oates, the Pulitzer Prize–nominated author, has stepped up to defend Nolan’s interpretation. “One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful & respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is,” Oates wrote on X.

I can’t pretend to be as knowledgeable as any of these scholars, filmmakers and authors, but I did like the movie and the fact that it’s introducing this type of literature and history to a whole new audience. And in the end, isn’t that what it’s all about?
